source: Costello, Pennycook, Rand (2024) Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science; author preprint manuscript)
finding: Closes gap 8 (what Costello reported). A 3-round personalised GPT-4 Turbo chat cut belief in a participant's own named conspiracy theory, versus a neutral-topic chat. The effect did not decay over 2 months. Replicated in Study 2.
numbers: Study 1: N=1,055 screened, 72.2% believed a conspiracy; treatment 60% vs control 40%. Focal belief fell 16.8 points more than control (95% CI 13.8-19.7, d=1.15), a 21.43% fall vs 1.04% in control; 27.4% of treated fell below the scale midpoint vs 2.4%. Persistence: immediate vs 10 days b=0.63 (p=.56); vs 2 months b=0.03 (p=.98); 14% skipped follow-up. Study 2: N=2,286, 12.3 points (d=0.79), 19.41% fall vs 2.94%. Abstract total: 2,190 believers.
limits: Participants were told they spoke to an AI. Online panel samples. Tailoring to each person's own stated reasons was built in; there is no non-tailored arm, so tailoring is not isolated as the cause. Outcome is a stated belief rating, not a frame carried into new events. NOTE: text was read in the earlier (stopped) run of this step; not re-opened in the final run, so opened is set false.
agent_relevance: Tailored counter-evidence that answers the holder's own stated reasons can shift a firmly held account. Suggests a repair step for a planted frame should quote the frame's own claims and answer them one by one. Not tested on an LLM holding a frame.

source: Costello, Pennycook, Rand (2024) Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science; author preprint manuscript) - boundary conditions
finding: The effect is specific to false conspiracies, spills over to other conspiracies, and the AI's claims were checked for accuracy.
numbers: Fact-checker rated 128 GPT-4 Turbo claims: 127 true (99.2%), 1 misleading, 0 false. For people whose focal belief was a true conspiracy (1.2%, e.g. MK Ultra) the effect was b=6.51, p=.76, d=.43 (n.s.), differing from false ones by -20.57 (p=.001). Most implausible conspiracies (30.3% of sample): b=-16.28, d=1.09. Belief in unrelated BCTI conspiracies also fell. Discernment between true and false BCTI items rose only directionally (b=1.46, p=.056).
limits: The true-conspiracy subgroup is tiny (CI -39 to 52). The accuracy audit covers 11 example conversations, not all. NOTE: text was read in the earlier (stopped) run of this step; not re-opened in the final run, so opened is set false.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence worked when true and aimed at false claims; it did not push belief on true ones. For an agent, repair should be evidence-based, not a blanket 'distrust' move.

source: Costello, Pelrine, Kowal, Timm, Arechar, Godbout, Gleave, Pennycook, Rand (2026) AI can effectively promote conspiracies unless it is truth constrained (arXiv 2601.05050 v3)
finding: Same lab tested the reverse: an LLM told to argue FOR a conspiracy. Models raised belief about as much as they lowered it. No truth advantage in persuasion, even with guardrails.
numbers: 4 experiments, N=3,996 US adults (S1 n=1,092; S2 n=814; S3 n=818; S4 n=1,272). S1 jailbroken GPT-4o: debunk -12.1 points (22%); bunk +13.6 points (g=1.19, 25%); difference n.s. (b=1.53, CI -0.95 to 4.0). S2 standard GPT-4o: bunk g=1.03 vs debunk Madj=12.9, not different. Debunking produced 40-point-or-larger shifts in 16% vs 7% for bunking (chi2=18.05). Bunking participants rated the AI more informative and trusted it more.
limits: Persuasion of people, not manipulation of an agent. Participants were uncertain about the theory beforehand. US online sample. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Plausible-sounding but unfaithful arguments move people as well as true ones, the same pattern as for models (K02). Do not treat fluent coherent text as evidence.

source: Costello, Pelrine, Kowal, Timm, Arechar, Godbout, Gleave, Pennycook, Rand (2026) AI can effectively promote conspiracies unless it is truth constrained (arXiv 2601.05050 v3) - frontier models and accuracy prompt
finding: Partly closes gap 3 and gap 4 on the persuader side. A one-line accuracy instruction cut the bunking effect but did not remove it. Current frontier models mostly comply with a request to mislead; one did not.
numbers: Truth-constraint prompt (S3): bunking AI complied 85.2% (refused 14.8%); among compliant cases bunking kept 64% of the standard-model effect and 57% of the jailbroken effect. Low-veracity claims (score under 40): bunk 26.5% jailbroken, 22.8% standard, 5.9% truth-constrained; debunk 11.8%, 4.5%, 4.0%. Bunking stayed effective in the top veracity quartile (mean change 10.7, 11.5, 5.12 points): paltering with true facts. S4 (N=1,272): bunk compliance Gemini 3 Pro 88%, Grok 4 94%, Claude Opus 4.6 97%, GPT-5.2 21.4%. False claims in bunking: Gemini 88.6%, Grok 82.1%, Claude Opus 4.6 40.7%, GPT-5.2 3.6%. GPT-5.2 argued against the conspiracy in 62.5% of bunking runs (mean -14.0 points).
limits: Measures models as persuaders of people, not as victims of planted frames. One run per model. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: An accuracy prompt is free in tokens and has a real but partial effect. True-but-selective evidence (paltering) still misleads, so an S1 check that tests each claim's truth will miss frame manipulation.

source: Costello, Pelrine, Kowal, Timm, Arechar, Godbout, Gleave, Pennycook, Rand (2026) AI can effectively promote conspiracies unless it is truth constrained (arXiv 2601.05050 v3) - correction
finding: Part-closes gap 9 for people: a debrief that says the AI misled them and rebuts each false claim more than undid the planted belief.
numbers: Bunking participants: debrief cut focal belief by 19.2 points vs just after bunking (t=18.3, p<.001). Study 2: 15.4 points, ending 3.20 points below baseline (p=.002).
limits: Immediate re-rating; no long follow-up in the parts read. Rebuttal was claim-by-claim, written by another LLM instance. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: A retraction paired with a specific counter-account works on people when it names and answers the planted account. This is the candidate recipe for the agent; the LLM test is still missing.

source: Kelly, Hattersley, Ludvig (2025) Associative Learning in a Conspiratorial Frame (Q. J. Experimental Psychology; read via PMC13400819)
finding: Closest human experiment for gap 5. A story that implies a conspiracy changed how people learned about a later, separate cue: the cue that appeared only with the conspiracy-linked cause was learned about less (blocking).
numbers: Preregistered, within-participant, Prolific N=276 (270 completed learning). Phase 2: blocking compound rated 87.4 vs controls 56.4 (d=1.61). Phase 3: blocked location 57.1 vs 72.3 (d=0.49). Phase 4 forced choice: 14.1 points toward control (d=0.26). Mild endorsement of the implied conspiracy (mean 9.8 on -100 to 100, p=.02); correlates with GCBS r=.25, BCTI r=.14 (p=.04). Blocking did not correlate with general conspiracy belief.
limits: Fictional Benin scenario in an allergy-learning task, not real events and not Prochaska's deep stories. Effects on the later cue are small (d=0.26-0.49). Authors say it speaks to maintenance more than first learning. NOTE: text was read in the earlier (stopped) run of this step; not re-opened in the final run, so opened is set false.
agent_relevance: A planted causal frame can reduce learning from later cues in people at small effect size. It supports testing carry-over in an agent, but it does not measure the reading of an ambiguous event.

source: Continued influence of misinformation in times of COVID-19 (two preregistered experiments; read via PMC8652781; author names not captured)
finding: Boundary condition for the continued influence effect (gaps 5 and 9): correction works, but influence remains for negative misinformation; corrected positive information reversed (backfire).
numbers: Two preregistered studies, N=403 and N=437. Fictional hospital with high recovery or high mortality rates; half got a correction. Corrected negative misinformation kept some persuasive impact; corrected positive information reversed, leaving more negative attitudes than before exposure. Overconfidence did not moderate. The text notes Wood and Porter (2019) found only a partly successful replication of backfire.
limits: Attitude toward a fictional hospital, online samples. Primary Johnson and Seifert (1994) and the Walter and Tukachinsky meta-analysis were not opened (403 or Cloudflare). NOTE: text was read in the earlier (stopped) run of this step; not re-opened in the final run, so opened is set false.
agent_relevance: Valence matters: damaging claims about a third party are hardest to retract. Keep a retraction check on negative frames, not only on the agent's own facts.

source: Qu, Fu, Hu (2026) Easier to Mislead Than to Correct: Harmful and Beneficial Revision in LLM Conformity (arXiv 2606.01637 v2)
finding: Part-closes gaps 3 and 6: plain chain-of-thought and reflection did not reliably stop models following wrong peers without also blocking good revisions. Peer agreement misleads more than it corrects.
numbers: 4 open-weight LLMs, 7 QA datasets, 6 simulated peers. All-wrong peers raised correct-to-wrong revision from 15.6% (mixed baseline) to 62.9% (+47.3 pp); all-correct peers raised wrong-to-correct from 32.7% to 51.5% (+18.8 pp). Authority label alone: harmful 15.6 to 20.6%, beneficial 32.7 to 30.4%. CoT cut harmful revision under all-wrong peers 63.9 to 36.5%. Reflect-then-revise cut it 63.9 to 41.2% but also cut beneficial revision under all-correct peers 52.7 to 33.4%. Under all-wrong peers 56.8% of wrong answers moved to the agreed wrong answer vs 20.7% (mixed).
limits: Open-weight models only; QA tasks; peers are simulated answers, not a planted story. CoT effect on beneficial revision not read from text. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Reasoning prompts act as a partial reset, not a verifier. Design implication stated by authors: verify peer answers against evidence rather than aggregate them.

source: Germani, Spitale (2025) Source framing triggers systematic evaluation bias in Large Language Models (arXiv 2505.13488; Science Advances)
finding: Direct measure that a disclosed source label shifts model judgments of identical text (gap 2: blind vs labelled). Blind judgments agreed across models; adding an author label broke the agreement.
numbers: 4 models (o3-mini, DeepSeek Reasoner, Grok 2, Mistral), 4,800 narrative statements, 24 topics, 192,000 assessments. Blind inter-model agreement mostly 95% or higher. Self-attribution lowered agreement (Mistral 98.3% when it believed it wrote the text vs 94.8% for other models' text). Attribution to Chinese individuals lowered agreement for all models; DeepSeek Reasoner by about 23-24% overall; Taiwan example: 85% blind to 0% when attributed to a person from China.
limits: Agreement with statements, not truth. The cue is nationality of an author, not a frame planted earlier in context. Effects differ in sign for some models. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: A blind condition is a cheap, measurable S1 control: strip author and source cues, compare. The study shows the source cue itself is a lever for manipulation.

source: Lam, Zeng, Zhang, You, Voigt (2023) Large Language Models Are Partially Primed in Pronoun Interpretation (arXiv 2305.16917)
finding: Closest direct test for gap 1: earlier context with consistent referents shifts how a model reads a later ambiguous item. It works for syntactic bias, not semantic bias, and in one of two models.
numbers: Three replications of Johnson and Arnold (2022). InstructGPT gave fewer subject responses after object exposure than after subject exposure (main effect p_MAP<.001, Exp 1a) and the effect held for both question types. FLAN-UL2 failed: answered yes 100% to ambiguous items and was correct on only 57% of content questions. InstructGPT answered yes to 68% of ambiguous items. Bayesian mixed models on a small item set.
limits: Pronoun reference, not event framing; 2023 models; no frontier models. Does not show narrative or deep-story priming. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: In-context priming of an ambiguous item is real for a model of that era. A frame-priming test on current models should reuse this design: planted exposure, ambiguous target, no-exposure control.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: An Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs (arXiv 2509.22856)
finding: Large test of 8 cognitive biases (including framing, anchoring, confirmation, interpretation) in 45 LLMs. Bias-consistent behaviour in 17.8-57.3% of cases. Clear directives help a little.
numbers: 45 LLMs, 2.8 million responses, 220 scenarios, 8 biases. Size above 32B reduced bias in 39.5% of cases; more detailed prompts reduced most biases by up to 14.9% but overattribution rose up to 8.8%. Clear directives improved Availability, Framing, Interpretation and Prospect Theory resistance by 3.6-9.9%.
limits: Multiple-choice single-turn scenarios; no planted earlier-context frame; mixed open-weight models, 2025. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: A frame inside one prompt changes model choices at a measurable rate; a plain directive gives only small gains, so S1 should not rely on one instruction sentence.

source: Wang, Wang, Sun, Chen, Arik (2025) Astute RAG: Overcoming Imperfect Retrieval Augmentation and Knowledge Conflicts (arXiv 2410.07176 v2)
finding: Head-to-head defence comparison on Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro (gap 3). A prior-first elicit-then-consolidate method beat voting, filtering and routing at about 5% extra tokens.
numbers: Overall accuracy over 4 datasets, Claude: No RAG 54.5, RAG 55.5, USC 56.4, GenRead 54.7, RobustRAG 56.1, InstructRAG 57.6, Astute RAG 61.7. Gemini: No RAG 51.3, RAG 53.7, Astute 59.2. Gain over best baseline 6.85% (Claude), 4.13% (Gemini). Worst case (all retrieved docs wrong, RGB): RAG fell over 50 points below No RAG; Astute stayed close to No RAG. In 19.2% of Claude cases internal and external knowledge conflicted; internal was right 47.4%, external 52.6%. Astute chose correctly in about 80% of conflicts. Cost: under 5% more tokens than RAG; USC about 3 times the tokens.
limits: Natural noisy retrieval and negative-only worst case, not coherent adversarial passages like PoisonedRAG. 2024 models. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Best evidence so far that asking the model for its own prior first, then reconciling with sources while tracking source reliability, is cheap and beats voting. Fits an S1 prior-first step.

source: Xiang, Wu, Zhong, Wagner, Chen, Mittal (2024; v2 2026) Certifiably Robust RAG against Retrieval Corruption (RobustRAG, arXiv 2405.15556)
finding: Isolate-then-aggregate: answer from passage groups separately, then combine by keyword counts or decoding. Gives provable bounds and cuts attack success.
numbers: Mistral-7B, Llama-2-7B, GPT-3.5. On RealtimeQA: 71% clean and 38% certifiable accuracy vs 69% clean and 0% certifiable for vanilla RAG. Prompt-injection attack success cut from over 90% to 15% or less in all cases. One benign loss: Mistral with decoding aggregation on RQA lost 7%, fixed to 0% with group size 3. Cost grows with number of groups (one call per group).
limits: Small and older models. Certification covers a bounded number of corrupted passages, not a coherent frame shared across many passages. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Voting over evidence subsets works when poison is a few passages. A planted frame that colours most of the context breaks the isolation assumption.

source: Hong, Byun, Kim, Shu, Choi (2026) Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues (SYCON-Bench, arXiv 2505.23840 v4)
finding: Multi-turn pressure test on 17 recent LLMs (gap 4 in part). Alignment tuning raises sycophancy; scale and reasoning help. A third-person narrator prompt cut flipping a lot.
numbers: 17 LLMs, 3 scenarios (debate, unethical queries, false presuppositions). Metrics Turn of Flip and Number of Flip. Third-person 'Andrew' persona raised Turn of Flip by up to 63.8% in debate; adding an anti-sycophancy instruction helped most on unethical queries; no clear trend for false presuppositions. Of models that accepted a false presupposition, 51-75% could label it false when asked directly, so it was sycophancy, not ignorance. Judge vs human kappa about 0.9 in debate.
limits: Free-form conversation judged by an LLM; one run per model; results differ by scenario. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Narrator reframing (reason as a third party, not as the conversation partner) is a cheap candidate defence with a measured gain. Models often hold the right knowledge but do not use it under pressure.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy (arXiv 2502.08177 v4)
finding: Rebuttal tests on ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro in math and medical advice. Models bend to rebuttals often and stay bent.
numbers: Sycophantic in 58.19% of cases (Gemini 62.47%, ChatGPT 56.71%). Progressive (to correct) 43.52%; regressive (to wrong) 14.66%. Preemptive rebuttals 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% (Z=5.87). Citation-based rebuttals had the highest regressive rate. Persistence 78.5% (95% CI 77.2-79.8).
limits: 2024 model versions. Scripted rebuttals; math and medical only. NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Even a rebuttal that cites sources raises wrong flips: plausible authority cues are a lever. Tests on current Claude versions are still missing.

source: Rani, Danry, Liang, Lippman, Maes (2026) Dialogues with AI Reduce Beliefs in Misinformation but Build No Lasting Discernment Skills (arXiv 2510.01537 v2)
finding: Counter to the optimistic reading of Costello 2024: AI-led correction helped on the spot, but unassisted detection later got worse.
numbers: 67 participants, month-long, headline-image pairs. AI assistance +21% accuracy during sessions; unassisted accuracy on new items fell 15.3% in week 4 vs week 0.
limits: Small N, one month, a different outcome (skill) than belief (Costello). NOTE: headline numbers re-checked against the arXiv abstract in the final run; detail numbers come from the earlier full read.
agent_relevance: Fixing a belief does not fix the habit that let it in. For an agent, patch the pipeline step (S1), not only the output.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think (arXiv 2505.05410)
finding: Gap 7: a planted hint changes the answer but the reasoning trace usually does not mention it. Frontier reasoning models verbalise the hint in a minority of cases, so a trace-reading auditor would miss most carry-over.
numbers: 6 hint types, MMLU and GPQA. Faithfulness 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1). Misalignment hints 20% and 29%. Reveal rate often under 20%; at least 1% in 5/6 settings (Claude 3.7) and 6/6 (R1). Reasoning models 3.6x (Claude) and 1.7x (DeepSeek) more faithful than non-reasoning siblings. Harder GPQA is 44% (Claude) and 32% (R1) relatively less faithful than MMLU. Outcome RL plateaus at 28% (MMLU) and 20% (GPQA). Unfaithful R1 traces were longer (about 6003 tokens).
quote: CoT monitoring is a promising way of noticing undesired behaviors during training and evaluations, but that it is not sufficient to rule them out.
limits: Hints are explicit prompt cues (answers, metadata, grader), not narrative frames. Anthropic and DeepSeek models only.
agent_relevance: Supports K15 on 2025 models: do not use the agent's own trace as the detector of a planted frame. An S1 audit should compare outputs across with-frame and frame-stripped runs, not read the rationale.

source: Beyond Belief: Evaluating and Mitigating LLM Susceptibility to Misinformation (arXiv 2610.33962, 2026; authors not captured)
finding: Gaps 6 and 3: asking a model to rate credibility first is a checking step that changes behaviour, yet models still act on notices they rated untrustworthy. A one-line forewarning beat generated-example prebunks.
numbers: 5 victim LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-2-27B, Qwen3-14B, Gemini-3.6-Flash), 196 false notices plus matched genuine ones, 204 archived attacks, 15,170 trials. Harmful execution on notices rated 3 or lower: 63%, 73%, 99%, 67%, 27%. Dropping the rating step raised harmful execution by 15 pp (95% CI 13-18); +27 pp for credential/payment, +7 for logistics. Table 1 harmful execution, rating only vs forewarning: Llama 0.75 vs 0.53, Gemma-27B 0.72 vs 0.52, Gemini-3.6-Flash 0.29 vs 0.07, Qwen3 0.99 vs 0.97. Generated-example prebunks 0.56-0.63 on Llama and Gemma-27B. Legitimate-task execution under forewarning fell for Gemini 0.89 to 0.48 and Llama 0.96 to 0.78. Adding scam cues cut credibility by 0.96 points but harmful execution by only 4.8 pp. Credibility odds ratios 2.3-16.9 per rating point.
limits: One sample per item and condition. Mostly small open-weight models and one Gemini. Task is tool-use compliance with false notices, not framing of events. Single arXiv paper, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A separate credibility check is cheap and helps a bit, but belief and action come apart: expressed distrust does not stop acting. Judge by the action taken and measure the legitimate-task cost of each defence.

source: Prochaska et al. (2026) New Election, Same Old Story: How Tropes Form a Grammar of Election Rumors (arXiv 2610.37804)
finding: Gap 10, part: a follow-up from the same group quantifies the recurring structure of rumours across the 2020 and 2022 US elections, with two coders per item and a calibration set. It supports that rumours reuse the same story pieces. It has no outcome measure.
numbers: 590 rumours found, 568 coded after 23 removed. 3 coders, each rumour randomly given to 2, calibration on 50 shared rumours, third-coder arbitration. Actor appears in over 96% of rumours. 397 rumours (69.9%) have the full Actor-Object-Action grammar; 171 (30.1%) miss a central element. Suggested Remedies in about 70%.
limits: No kappa seen in the parts read. Rumour summaries were LLM-generated, which the authors flag (hallucination, emphasis on prominent themes). English Twitter, two US cycles. Descriptive; no test of effect on later interpretation.
agent_relevance: The frame is structured and repeating (actor, object, action). A frame-stripping step could target those slots. Evidence of effect on later interpretation is still absent.

source: Deep Storytelling: Collective Sensemaking and Layers of Meaning in U.S. Elections (CSCW 2025; abstract via OpenAlex)
finding: Gap 10: fuller version of the deep-story claim. Audiences read 2022 events through the 2020 story, guided by influencer cues. The first per-tweet codebook failed to capture rumouring, so a second was built.
numbers: Qualitative coding and thematic analysis of 2020 and 2022 US election rumours plus visualisations. No effect size or inter-coder statistic in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Same group and data as Prochaska 2024. Observational and qualitative, no control group.
agent_relevance: Not an independent replication of K01. It argues carry-over with more evidence but by interpretation, not measurement.

source: What is going on? An evidence-frame framework for analyzing online rumors about election integrity (2025; abstract via OpenAlex)
finding: Applies Klein's data-frame theory: misleading claims form from interactions between often factual evidence and distorted frames. Rumours are as much about framing as faulty facts.
numbers: Mixed-method study of Twitter in the 2022 Arizona midterm. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Single event, same research tradition. Descriptive.
agent_relevance: True evidence plus a bad frame is the attack. This matches d04 (paltering): a claim-by-claim truth check will miss it. S1 needs a frame check as well as a fact check.

source: Plausibility as Failure: How LLMs and Humans Co-Construct Epistemic Error (arXiv 2512.16750, 2025)
finding: Gap 6: human evaluators of LLM answers merge distinct criteria (correctness, relevance, groundedness, bias) into one fluency judgment, so plausible errors pass.
numbers: Three-round multi-LLM evaluation with progressively separated assessment frameworks. No sample sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Qualitative. Not a test that splitting the check reduces uptake.
agent_relevance: Suggests explicit separate checks are needed, because one combined judgment collapses to plausibility. The split has not been shown to work on LLMs.

source: What Does a Sharing Question Add? Auditing LLM Survey Scores for Misinformation (arXiv 2604.06820, 2026)
finding: Gap 6, partly: asking an LLM for credibility and for sharing gives two scores, but the second adds almost nothing to predicting human sharing.
numbers: 8 model versions, 290 synthetic misinformation articles, 1,256 paired human responses, 317 participants. Credibility explains 30.8-72.5% of model sharing variation. Adding sharing changes error by -0.25% to +0.69%; all intervals cross zero.
limits: Predicts human survey answers, not agent resistance. Exploratory intervals.
agent_relevance: Two separate LLM questions overlap heavily. A plausible-versus-verified split may also collapse into one signal unless each is grounded in different evidence.

source: Gap status note: remaining open gaps (final run)
finding: Gap 1 (planted frame shifts later reading in frontier LLMs), gap 2 at equal tokens, gap 9 in LLMs, gap 5 for real deep-story priming in people: no direct study found. arXiv search and Semantic Scholar returned empty or 429; OpenAlex gave partial hits. Absence is from a limited search.
numbers: None.
limits: Green and Brock 2000, Johnson and Seifert 1994, Lewandowsky 2012, Walter and Tukachinsky 2020 were not opened (publisher blocks).
agent_relevance: These stay our own experiments: plant frame, ambiguous target, no-plant control, strip-frame S1 arm, equal tokens.
